**Muscadelle** is a white wine grape variety. It has a simple aroma of grape juice and raisins like grapes of the Muscat family of grapes, but it is unrelated. 


DNA analysis has indicated that Muscadelle is a cross between Gouais blanc and an unidentified grape variety.[1]



## Wine regions

[edit]

In France, it is a minor constituent in the dry and sweet wines of Bordeaux, such as Sauternes. It rarely makes up more than 10% of the blend, which is dominated by Sémillon and Sauvignon blanc. Throughout the 1990s and the beginning of the 21st century, plantings of the grape were falling. Some sweet wines from Monbazillac, on the other hand, can have a higher proportion of Muscadelle.


In Australia, the grape is used to make a fortified wine, now known as Topaque (formerly Tokay). Those made in the Rutherglen region generally receive considerable aging in hot cellars, leading to a maderised and oxidative character. A few other Australian wine regions, including the Barossa Valley, make similar wines. A few other Australian wineries use Muscadelle to make table wines in a similar way to French wineries. In accordance with an agreement reached with the EU, Australian producers phased out their use of the term Tokay by 2020, most choosing instead the name *Topaque* to represent this style.[2]


The name, Tokay, convinced some Australian producers that the grape was Pinot gris (which used to be called Tokay by producers in Alsace). Others thought the grape might have been Hárslevelű, one of the components of the famous Hungarian sweet wine Tokaji. However, it has been proven that Australian Tokay is Muscadelle.[*by whom?*]



## Synonyms

[edit]

Muscadelle is also known under the synonyms Angelicaut, Angelico, Blanc Cadillac, Blanche Douce, Bouillenc Muscat, Buillenc, Cadillac, Catape, Colle, Colle Musquette, Doucanelle, Douzanelle, Enfin, Guepie, Guilan Doux, Guilan Muscat, Guilan Musque, Guillan, Guillan Musque, Guinlhan Musque, Marmesie, Marseillais, Muscade, Muscadela, Muscadelle de Bordelais, Muscadet, Muscadet Doux, Muscalea, Muscat Fou, Musquette, Pedro Ximenes Krimsky, Raisimotte, Raisin de Musco, Raisinote, Raisinotte, Rousselou, Sauvignon à Gros Grains, Sauvignon Muscadelle, Sauvignon vert, Tokay, Vesparo, and White Angelica.[1]

<fragment>
Red wine produced under the **Bordeaux AOC** is made mostly from Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, with the addition of Cabernet Franc and small amounts of Petit Verdot, Malbec and Carmenère. This appellation covers around 42,600 hectares of vines and produces around 223 million litres of wine (which is nearly a third of the total wine production of Bordeaux).[5] White wine produced under the **Bordeaux Sec AOC** is made mostly from Sauvignon blanc and Sémillon, with the addition of some Muscadelle, Colombard, Mauzac, Merlot blanc, Ondenc and Ugni blanc.[6] It must contain no more than 4g/L of residual sugar. 
</fragment>
<fragment>
Wine growing areas in France

This article is about the various different regions, or AOCs, which lie within the wine region of Bordeaux. For the wine generally, see Bordeaux wine.

The **wine regions of Bordeaux** are a large number of wine growing areas, differing widely in size and sometimes overlapping, which lie within the overarching wine region of Bordeaux, centred on the city of Bordeaux and covering the whole area of the Gironde department of Aquitaine.


The Bordeaux region is naturally divided by the Gironde Estuary into a Left Bank area which includes the Médoc and Graves and a Right Bank area which includes the Libournais, Bourg and Blaye. The Médoc is itself divided into Haut-Médoc (the upstream or southern portion) and Bas-Médoc (the downstream or northern portion, often referred to simply as "Médoc").


</fragment>
<fragment>
This appellation covers around 6500 hectares of vines and 38 million litres of wine.[7] If it has more than 4g/L of residual sugar, then it may be labelled as **Bordeaux Molleux AOC**, but little wine is in fact produced under this AOC.[8] **Bordeaux Supérieur AOC** covers both red and white wines, and the grapes used are the same, but permitted yields are slightly lower, minimum alcohol content is slightly higher and slightly longer aging is required.[9] The amount of red wine produced under this appellation (around 45 million litres, from 10,000 hectares of vines) is much greater than the amount of white wine produced (around 170,000 litres from 60 hectares).[10]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Both red and white Bordeaux wines are almost invariably blended. The permissible grape varieties in red Bordeaux are: Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petit Verdot. While wine making styles vary, a rule of thumb is that the Left Bank is predominantly Cabernet Sauvignon based with the Right Bank being more Merlot based. The Graves area produces both red wine (from the grapes previously mentioned) and white wine from the Sauvignon blanc, Sémillon and Muscadelle grapes. The area of Sauternes (including Barsac) is known for its botrytized dessert wines.[2]

Based on my research of the Wikipedia articles on Bordeaux wines and grape varieties, I can provide you with a comprehensive overview of the key grape varieties used in Bordeaux wine production.

## **Red Grape Varieties**

### **Principal Varieties:**

1. **Cabernet Sauvignon**
   - Most widely planted grape in Bordeaux as of 2015
   - Cross between Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc (originated in the 17th century)
   - Thick skins, hardy vines, naturally low yielding
   - Particularly prominent on the Left Bank (Médoc)
   - Resistant to rot, buds late to avoid frost

2. **Merlot**
   - Became the most widely planted grape in Bordeaux after the 1852 powdery mildew epidemic devastated Cabernet Sauvignon
   - Dominant on the Right Bank (Libournais)

3. **Cabernet Franc**
   - One of the major black grape varieties worldwide
   - Parent of Cabernet Sauvignon (crossed with Sauvignon Blanc)
   - Used for blending with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot in Bordeaux style
   - Known locally as "Bouchet"
   - Can also be vinified alone, particularly in the Loire

### **Secondary Varieties:**

4. **Petit Verdot**
5. **Malbec** 
6. **Carmenère**

---

## **White Grape Varieties**

### **Principal White Varieties:**

1. **Sauvignon Blanc**
   - One of only four white grapes allowed in white Bordeaux wine
   - Principal grape in Château Margaux's Pavillon Blanc
   - Used mostly as a blending grape
   - Known for spicy, floral and mineral flavors in Loire, fruitier in Bordeaux

2. **Sémillon**
   - One of only three approved white wine varieties in Bordeaux
   - Essential for sweet wines like Sauternes (when affected by Botrytis/noble rot)
   - Heavy wines with low acidity and almost oily texture
   - High yield, can age for long periods
   - Thin skin, best suited to areas with sunny days and cool nights

3. **Muscadelle**
   - Simple aroma reminiscent of grape juice and raisins (unrelated to Muscat family)
   - Minor constituent in both dry and sweet Bordeaux wines (rarely more than 10%)
   - Cross between Gouais blanc and an unidentified grape variety

### **Other White Grapes Used:**
- Colombard
- Mauzac
- Merlot blanc
- Ondenc
- Ugni blanc

---

## **Regional Characteristics**

- **Left Bank (Médoc, Graves)**: Predominantly Cabernet Sauvignon-based reds, produces both red and white wines
- **Right Bank (Libournais)**: More Merlot-based reds
- **Sauternes/Barsac**: Famous for botrytized dessert wines, primarily from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc, and Muscadelle

## **Bordeaux Blend Philosophy**

Bordeaux wines are almost invariably blended, allowing winemakers to balance the characteristics of different grape varieties. The blending tradition has been refined over centuries to create complex, age-worthy wines that reflect their specific terroir.

The combination of these grape varieties, particularly the balance between Cabernet Sauvignon's structure and Merlot's softness in reds, or Sauvignon Blanc's acidity with Sémillon's body in whites, is what makes Bordeaux wines so distinctive and widely emulated worldwide.

Average vintages produce over 700 million bottles of wine, ranging from large quantities of everyday table wine, to some of the most expensive and prestigious wines in the world. The vast majority of wine produced in Bordeaux is red (sometimes called "claret" in Britain), with sweet white wines (most notably Sauternes), dry whites, and (in much smaller quantities) rosé and sparkling wines (Crémant de Bordeaux) collectively making up the remainder. Bordeaux wine is made by more than 5,660 producers or *châteaux*. There are 65 appellations of Bordeaux wine.[2][3]




## History

The red grapes in the Bordeaux vineyard are Merlot (62% by area), Cabernet Sauvignon (25%), Cabernet Franc (12%) and a small amount of Petit Verdot, Malbec and Carménère (1% in total). The white grapes are Sémillon (54% by area), Sauvignon blanc (36%), Muscadelle (7%) and a small amount of Ugni blanc, Colombard and Folle blanche (3% in total).[2] Because of the generally humid Bordeaux climate, a variety of pests can cause a problem for the *vigneron*. In the past, this was counteracted by the widespread use of pesticides, although the use of natural methods has recently been gaining in popularity. The vines are generally trained in either single or double guyot. Hand-picking is preferred by most of the prestigious châteaux, but machine-harvesting is popular in other places.[13]

<title>Cabernet Sauvignon</title>
<fragment>

A common factor affecting Bordeaux wines' flavours is Cabernet Sauvignon's harvest yields. Throughout Bordeaux, there is a legal maximum permitted yield of 50 hectoliters (hl) per hectare (ha). With the aid of global warming and vigorous rootstocks, many Bordeaux vineyards can easily surpass 60 hl/ha, with some estates taking advantage of the legal loophole of *plafond limite de classement* ("ceiling limit classification") that permits higher yields during "exceptional" years. This has had an adverse effect on the quality of production from some producers who regularly use grapes harvested at excessive yields. In recent years there has been more of an emphasis on keeping yields low, particularly for an estate's *Grand vin*.[3]



#### Other French regions

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
DNA evidence has shown Cabernet Sauvignon is the result of crossing two other Bordeaux grape varieties— Cabernet franc and Sauvignon blanc— which has led grapevine historians, or *ampelographers*, to believe that the grape originated in Bordeaux. Early records indicate that the grape was widespread in the Médoc region during the 18th century. The loose berry clusters and thick skins of the grape provided an excellent resistance to rot in the sometimes wet maritime climate of Bordeaux. The grape continued to grow in popularity until the *Powdery mildew* epidemic of 1852 exposed Cabernet Sauvignon's sensitivity to that grape disease. With vineyards severely ravaged or lost, many Bordeaux wine growers turned to Merlot, increasing its plantings to where it soon became the most widely planted grape in Bordeaux.

However, by 2015, Cabernet Sauvignon had once again become the most widely planted wine grape, with a total of 341,000 hectares (3,410 km2) under vine worldwide.[2]


Despite its prominence in the industry, the grape is a relatively new variety, the product of a chance crossing between Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon blanc during the 17th century in southwestern France. Its popularity is often attributed to its ease of cultivation—the grapes have thick skins and the vines are hardy and naturally low yielding, budding late to avoid frost and resistant to viticultural hazards such as rot and insects—and to its consistent presentation of structure and flavours which express the typical character ("typicity") of the variety. Familiarity has helped sell Cabernet Sauvignon wines to consumers, even from unfamiliar wine regions. Its widespread popularity has also contributed to criticism of the grape as a "colonizer" that takes over wine regions at the expense of indigenous grape varieties.[3]

<document>
<title>Bordeaux</title>
<fragment>
![](image)Château Haut-Brion
The vine was introduced to the Bordeaux region by the Romans, probably in the mid-first century, to provide wine for local consumption, and wine production has been continuous in the region since.[33]



![](image)Saint-Émilion aerial view
Bordeaux wine growing area has about 116,160 hectares (287,000 acres) of vineyards, 57 appellations, 10,000 wine-producing estates (châteaux) and 13,000 grape growers. With an annual production of approximately 960 million bottles,[34] the Bordeaux area produces large quantities of everyday wine as well as some of the most expensive wines in the world. Included among the latter are the area's five *premier cru* (First Growth) red wines (four from Médoc and one, Château Haut-Brion, from Graves), established by the Bordeaux Wine Official Classification of 1855:


</fragment>
<fragment>

Both red and white wines are made in the Bordeaux region. Red Bordeaux wine is called claret in the United Kingdom. Red wines are generally made from a blend of grapes, and may be made from Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Petit verdot, Malbec, and, less commonly in recent years, Carménère.


White Bordeaux is made from Sauvignon blanc, Sémillon, and Muscadelle. Sauternes is a sub-region of Graves known for its intensely sweet, white, dessert wines such as Château d'Yquem.


Because of a wine glut (wine lake) in the generic production, the price squeeze induced by an increasingly strong international competition, and vine pull schemes, the number of growers has recently dropped from 14,000 and the area under vine has also decreased significantly. In the meantime, the global demand for first growths and the most famous labels markedly increased and their prices skyrocketed.[*citation needed*]

Bordeaux is a major centre for business in France as it has the sixth largest metropolitan population in France. It serves as a major regional center for trade, administration, services and industry.

<fragment>
![](image)Merlot grapes being sorted at Château Kirwan
The red grapes in the Bordeaux vineyard are Merlot (62% by area), Cabernet Sauvignon (25%), Cabernet Franc (12%) and a small amount of Petit Verdot, Malbec and Carménère (1% in total). The white grapes are Sémillon (54% by area), Sauvignon blanc (36%), Muscadelle (7%) and a small amount of Ugni blanc, Colombard and Folle blanche (3% in total).[2] Because of the generally humid Bordeaux climate, a variety of pests can cause a problem for the *vigneron*. In the past, this was counteracted by the widespread use of pesticides, although the use of natural methods has recently been gaining in popularity. The vines are generally trained in either single or double guyot. Hand-picking is preferred by most of the prestigious châteaux, but machine-harvesting is popular in other places.[13]



### Winemaking

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In Bordeaux the concept of *terroir* plays a pivotal role in wine production with the top estates aiming to make *terroir* driven wines that reflect the place they are from, often from grapes collected from a single vineyard.[11] The soil of Bordeaux is composed of gravel, sandy stone, and clay. The region's best vineyards are located on the well-drained gravel soils that are frequently found near the Gironde river. An old adage in Bordeaux is the best estates can "see the river" from their vineyards. The majority of land facing riverward is occupied by classified estates.[11]



## Grapes

[edit]

### Reds

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
* *Sweet white wines*. In several locations and appellations throughout the region, sweet white wine is made from Sémillon, Sauvignon blanc and Muscadelle grapes affected by noble rot. The best-known of these appellations is Sauternes, which also has an official classification, and where some of the world's most famous sweet wines are produced. There are also appellations neighbouring Sauternes, on both sides of the Garonne river, where similar wines are made. These include Loupiac, Cadillac, and Sainte Croix du Mont. The regional appellation for sweet white wines is Bordeaux Supérieur Blanc.[23] In 2007, 3.2% of the region's vineyard surface was used for wines in this family.[17][18]


The vast majority of Bordeaux wine is red, with red wine production outnumbering white wine production six to one.[5]

### Terroir

[edit]

Main article: Terroir


</fragment>
<fragment>

Most varieties of grape are primarily associated with a certain region, such as Cabernet Sauvignon in Bordeaux and Syrah in Rhône, although there are some varieties that are found in two or more regions, such as Chardonnay in Bourgogne (including Chablis) and Champagne, and Sauvignon blanc in Loire and Bordeaux. As an example of the rules, although climatic conditions would appear to be favorable, no Cabernet Sauvignon wines are produced in Rhône, Riesling wines in Loire, or Chardonnay wines in Bordeaux. (If such wines were produced, they would have to be declassified to Vin de Pays or French table wine. They would not be allowed to display any appellation name or even region of origin.)


Traditionally, many French wines have been blended from several grape varieties. Varietal white wines have been, and are still, more common than varietal red wines.


At the 2007 harvest, the most common grape varieties were the following:[18][19]






</fragment>
<fragment>
* *Vin délimité de qualité supérieure* (VDQS, 0.9%) – Less strict than AOC, usually used for smaller areas or as a "waiting room" for potential AOCs. This category was abolished at the end of 2011.
* *Appellation d'origine contrôlée* (AOC, 53.4%) – Wine from a particular area with many other restrictions, including grape varieties and winemaking methods.[13]


The total French production for the 2005 vintage was 43.9 million hl (plus an additional 9.4 million hl destined for various brandies) of which 28.3% was white and 71.7% was red or rosé.[13] The proportion of white wine is slightly higher for the higher categories, with 34.3% of the AOC wine being white. In years with less favourable vintage conditions than 2005, the proportion of AOC wine tends to be a little lower. The proportion of *Vin de table* has decreased considerably over the last decades, while the proportion of AOC has increased somewhat and *Vin de Pays* has increased considerably. In 2005 there were 472 wine AOCs in France.[14]

<title>Regional Bordeaux AOCs</title>
<fragment>

Average yearly production is 3,300,000 hectolitres, corresponding to approximately 431 million 75 cl bottles, with 2,300,100 hectolitres of red wine[2] and 304,000 hectolitres of white wine.[3]


The maximal authorized yield for Bordeaux AOC is 55 hectoliter per hectare, and the alcohol level of the wine must be between 10 and 13 volume percent.[2] Dry white Bordeaux may not have more than 4 grams per litre of residual sugar.[3]



### Grape Varieties

[edit]

For red wines, the most planted grape varietals are Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon. As most regional Bordeaux AOC wines are produced on the Right Bank, Cabernet Franc is often found in the blend. Winemakers are using more and more Malbec,[4] but Petit Verdot is not often seen.


For white wines, Sauvignon blanc and Sémillon each represent 42% of the vineyard surface and Muscadelle 9%.[3]

The white grapes are Sémillon (54% by area), Sauvignon blanc (36%), Muscadelle (7%) and a small amount of Ugni blanc, Colombard and Folle blanche (3% in total).[2] Because of the generally humid Bordeaux climate, a variety of pests can cause a problem for the *vigneron*. In the past, this was counteracted by the widespread use of pesticides, although the use of natural methods has recently been gaining in popularity. The vines are generally trained in either single or double guyot. Hand-picking is preferred by most of the prestigious châteaux, but machine-harvesting is popular in other places.[13]



### Winemaking

[edit]


</fragment>

As of July 2019, Bordeaux wineries authorized the use of four new red grapes to combat effects of climate change on viticulture in Bordeaux. These newly approved grapes are Marselan, Touriga Nacional, Castets, and Arinarnoa.[14][15]

There are also appellations neighbouring Sauternes, on both sides of the Garonne river, where similar wines are made. These include Loupiac, Cadillac, and Sainte Croix du Mont. ## Key Findings from Wikipedia:

### From "French Wine" article (2007 data):
**France-wide grape variety statistics:**
- Merlot: 116,715 hectares total in France
- Cabernet Sauvignon: 57,913 hectares total in France  
- Cabernet Franc: 37,508 hectares total in France
- Sauvignon blanc: 26,062 hectares total in France
- Sémillon: 11,864 hectares total in France
- Muscadelle: 1,618 hectares total in France

### From "Bordeaux Wine" article:
- **Red vs White Production**: "The vast majority of Bordeaux wine is red, with red wine production outnumbering white wine production six to one"
- **Red grape percentages within red grapes**: Merlot (62%), Cabernet Sauvignon (25%), Cabernet Franc (12%), others (1%)
- **White grape percentages within white grapes**: Sémillon (54%), Sauvignon blanc (36%), Muscadelle (7%), others (3%)

### From "Regional Bordeaux AOCs" article:
- **Regional AOC breakdown**: Of approximately 61,700 hectares in regional AOCs:
  - Red wine: 50,000 hectares  
  - White wine: 6,740 hectares
  - **Red:White ratio in regional AOCs: ~7.4:1**

## Analysis and Calculations:

The key missing piece is the exact percentage of red vs. white plantings across ALL 116,160 hectares of Bordeaux. However, we can make informed estimates:

**If we use the 6:1 production ratio as a proxy for planted area:**
- Red grapes: approximately 98,000 hectares (84.3%)
- White grapes: approximately 18,160 hectares (15.6%)

**Then calculate individual varieties:**
- **Merlot**: 98,000 × 62% = **60,760 hectares**
- **Cabernet Sauvignon**: 98,000 × 25% = **24,500 hectares**  
- **Cabernet Franc**: 98,000 × 12% = **11,760 hectares**
- **Sémillon**: 18,160 × 54% = **9,806 hectares**
- **Sauvignon blanc**: 18,160 × 36% = **6,538 hectares**
- **Muscadelle**: 18,160 × 7% = **1,271 hectares**

## Limitations:
- The red:white ratio based on production may not perfectly match planted area ratios
- These are 2007 French statistics - more recent CIVB data would be preferable
- The calculations assume the red:white production ratio translates directly to planted area

## Recommendations:
For the most definitive statistics, I'd recommend:
1. **CIVB (Conseil Interprofessionnel du Vin de Bordeaux)** official website and annual reports
2. **French Ministry of Agriculture** wine sector statistics
3. **INAO (Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité)** vineyard registry data
4. **Eurostat** agricultural statistics database

article_title: International Organisation of Vine and Wine

msg.content:
<document>
<title>International Organisation of Vine and Wine</title>
<fragment>

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]




## History

[edit]

<fragment>
The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]



## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).


</fragment>
<fragment>

The current International Organisation of Vine and Wine was established following a 35-nation agreement on 3 April 2001, and replaced the International Vine and Wine Office. This agreement went into effect on 1 January 2004.[3]

article_title: International Organisation of Vine and Wine

msg.content:
<document>
<title>International Organisation of Vine and Wine</title>
<fragment>

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]




## History

[edit]

The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]



## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).


</fragment>

A common factor affecting Bordeaux wines' flavours is Cabernet Sauvignon's harvest yields. Throughout Bordeaux, there is a legal maximum permitted yield of 50 hectoliters (hl) per hectare (ha). With the aid of global warming and vigorous rootstocks, many Bordeaux vineyards can easily surpass 60 hl/ha, with some estates taking advantage of the legal loophole of *plafond limite de classement* ("ceiling limit classification") that permits higher yields during "exceptional" years. This has had an adverse effect on the quality of production from some producers who regularly use grapes harvested at excessive yields. Sémillon, which is relatively easy to cultivate,[3] consistently produces six to eight tons of grapes per acre from its vigorous vines.[4] It is fairly resistant to disease, except for rot. The grape ripens early, when, in warmer climates, it acquires a pinkish hue.[5] Since the grape has a thin skin, there is also a risk of sunburn in hotter climates; it is best suited to areas with sunny days and cool nights.


Sémillon wines are rather heavy, with low acidity and an almost oily texture. It has a high yield and wines based on it can age a long time. Along with Sauvignon blanc and Muscadelle, Sémillon is one of only three approved white wine varieties in the Bordeaux region.


The grape is also key to the production of sweet wines such as Sauternes. For the grapes to be used for sweet wine production, they need to have been affected by Botrytis (also known as "noble rot"). This fungus dries out the grapes, thus concentrating the sugar and flavours in the grape berry.

- **Cabernet Sauvignon**（赤霞珠）

I need help finding specific global acreage statistics for wine grape varieties. Please search for OIV (International Organisation of Vine and Wine) reports, global wine industry statistics, and agricultural data that provides:

1. The total global wine grape acreage and the top 10-15 varieties by worldwide acreage
2. Specific hectare numbers for major international varieties like Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Chardonnay, Airén, Tempranillo, Syrah/Shiraz, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir, Grenache, etc.
3. Recent data (2010s or 2020s) showing how these varieties rank globally
4. Statistics showing which varieties lead in terms of total worldwide planting

Please focus on finding authoritative sources like OIV annual reports, FAO agricultural statistics, wine industry research, and academic wine studies that discuss global varietal distribution and acreage.

This **list of grape varieties** includes cultivated grapes, whether used for wine, or eating as a table grape, fresh or dried (raisin, currant, sultana). For a complete list of all grape species including those unimportant to agriculture, see Vitis.


The term *grape variety* refers to cultivars rather than actual botanical varieties according to the International Code of Nomenclature for Cultivated Plants, because they are propagated by cuttings and may have unstable reproductive properties. However, the term *variety* has become so entrenched in viticulture that any change to using the term *cultivar* instead is unlikely.




## Single species grapes

[edit]

While some of the grapes in this list[1][2][3][4][5] are hybrids, they are hybridized within a single species. For those grapes hybridized across species, known as interspecific hybrids, see the section on multispecies hybrid grapes below.

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]




## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]

The current International Organisation of Vine and Wine was established following a 35-nation agreement on 3 April 2001, and replaced the International Vine and Wine Office. This agreement went into effect on 1 January 2004.[3]

The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).

![](image) A 50-yr old Airén vine, from a vineyard near Carabaña (Madrid, Spain)
**Airén** is a variety of *Vitis vinifera*, a white grape commonly used in winemaking. This grape is native to Spain where it represents almost a quarter of all grapes grown. As of 2010, Airén was estimated to be the world's 3rd most grown grape variety in terms of planted surface, at 252,000 hectares (620,000 acres), down from 306,000 hectares (760,000 acres) in 2004, where it held 1st place, although it is almost exclusively found in Spain.[1] Since Airén tends to be planted at a low density, several other varieties (including Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot) are more planted in terms of number of vines.

![](image) A 50-yr old Airén vine, from a vineyard near Carabaña (Madrid, Spain)
**Airén** is a variety of *Vitis vinifera*, a white grape commonly used in winemaking. This grape is native to Spain where it represents almost a quarter of all grapes grown. As of 2010, Airén was estimated to be the world's 3rd most grown grape variety in terms of planted surface, at 252,000 hectares (620,000 acres), down from 306,000 hectares (760,000 acres) in 2004, where it held 1st place, although it is almost exclusively found in Spain.[1] Since Airén tends to be planted at a low density, several other varieties (including Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot) are more planted in terms of number of vines.

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles for the major wine grape varieties you mentioned, here are their production regions and popular wine styles:

## **Chardonnay**
- **Origin**: France (Burgundy region)
- **Major Production Regions**: Widely grown globally with significant plantings in France (Burgundy, Champagne), United States (California, Oregon), Australia, Chile, South Africa, and New Zealand
- **Popular Wine Styles**: 
  - Crisp, unoaked white wines (Chablis-style)
  - Rich, buttery, oak-aged wines (California/Traditional Burgundy style)
  - Sparkling wines (Champagne and other méthode traditionnelle)
  - Aromas typically include green apple, citrus, tropical fruits, vanilla, and butter

## **Airén**
- **Origin**: Spain
- **Major Production Regions**: Almost exclusively grown in Spain, particularly in the La Mancha region
- **Popular Wine Styles**:
  - Light, fresh white wines with neutral character
  - Often used for bulk wine production and brandy making
  - Very high-yielding variety suitable for hot, arid climates
  - Typically produces wines with low acidity and simple fruit notes

## **Cabernet Sauvignon**
- **Origin**: France (Bordeaux region)
- **Major Production Regions**: Widely planted globally with major areas in France (Bordeaux), California (Napa Valley), Australia (Coonawarra), Chile, South Africa, and Italy
- **Popular Wine Styles**:
  - Full-bodied red wines with firm tannins
  - Often aged in oak barrels for complexity
  - Classic flavors include blackcurrant, blackberry, cedar, tobacco, and vanilla
  - Excellent aging potential, developing complex tertiary notes over time

## **Tempranillo**
- **Origin**: Spain
- **Major Production Regions**: Predominantly Spanish (Rioja, Ribera del Duero), but also grown in Portugal (where it's known as Tinta Roriz), Argentina, the United States, and Australia
- **Popular Wine Styles**:
  - Medium to full-bodied red wines
  - Often aged in oak (American oak in traditional Rioja, French oak in modern styles)
  - Flavors typically include red berries, leather, tobacco, vanilla, and earthy notes
  - Can be made in both youthful (joven) and aged (crianza, reserva, gran reserva) styles

Each variety's character is heavily influenced by its terroir (soil, climate, and winemaking traditions), leading to distinctive regional expressions of the same grape variety. Would you like more detailed information about any specific variety or wine region?

**Airén** is a variety of *Vitis vinifera*, a white grape commonly used in winemaking. This grape is native to Spain where it represents almost a quarter of all grapes grown. A common factor affecting Bordeaux wines' flavours is Cabernet Sauvignon's harvest yields. Throughout Bordeaux, there is a legal maximum permitted yield of 50 hectoliters (hl) per hectare (ha). With the aid of global warming and vigorous rootstocks, many Bordeaux vineyards can easily surpass 60 hl/ha, with some estates taking advantage of the legal loophole of *plafond limite de classement* ("ceiling limit classification") that permits higher yields during "exceptional" years. This has had an adverse effect on the quality of production from some producers who regularly use grapes harvested at excessive yields. Grenache is one of the most widely planted red wine grape varieties in the world with France and Spain being its largest principal wine regions. In the late 20th century, total acreage of Grenache in Spain has been on the decline with the vineyards being uprooted in lieu of the more fashionable Tempranillo, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot. Between the late 1980s and 2004, Spanish plantings dropped from 420,000 acres (170,000 ha) to 203,370 acres (82,300 ha) allowing France with its 236,500 acres (95,700 ha) to assume the mantle as the world's largest source of Grenache. As of 2000, Grenache was the third most widely planted red wine grape variety in France, behind Merlot and Carignan.[3] From French nurseries, Grenache has become the fourth most widely propagated vine with more than 23 million cuttings sold since 1998 according to French ampelographer Pierre Galet.[6]

Based on my search of Wikipedia articles, here are the key characteristics of five major wine grape varieties:

## 1. Cabernet Sauvignon
- **Origin**: France (Bordeaux region)
- **Wine Style**: Red wines known for full body, firm tannins, and dark fruit flavors
- **Growing Regions**: Worldwide, with major plantings in Bordeaux, California, Australia, and Chile
- **Notable Characteristics**: One of the most widely recognized and planted premium red grape varieties globally
- **Yield Management**: Quality heavily dependent on harvest yields - excessive yields (>60 hl/ha) can negatively impact wine quality

## 2. Chardonnay
- **Origin**: France (Burgundy region)
- **Wine Style**: White wines ranging from crisp and unoaked to rich and buttery with oak aging
- **Growing Regions**: Extensively planted - Burgundy, Champagne, California, Australia, New Zealand
- **Notable Characteristics**: Highly versatile - can produce everything from sparkling wines to full-bodied whites
- **Winemaking**: Response to oak aging significantly influences final style and flavors

## 3. Merlot
- **Origin**: France (Bordeaux region)
- **Wine Style**: Red wines with soft tannins, medium to full body, and ripe fruit flavors
- **Growing Regions**: One of the world's most planted grape varieties at 260,000+ hectares globally
- **Primary Use**: Essential component in Bordeaux blends (along with Cabernet Sauvignon) and produced as a varietal wine
- **Market Position**: Third most grown variety globally and one of the most popular red wine varietals in many markets

## 4. Tempranillo
- **Origin**: Spain (central and northern Spain)
- **Wine Style**: Red wines with medium to full body, flavors of red fruits, leather, and earthy notes
- **Growing Regions**: Dominant in Spain's Rioja and Ribera del Duero regions; expanding to Portugal, Argentina, and the Americas
- **Notable Characteristics**: Spain's "great indigenous grape variety" - the country's signature red grape
- **Aging**: Known for aging well, developing complexity in oak

## 5. Grenache (Garnacha)
- **Origin**: Spain (northeastern Spain)
- **Wine Style**: Red wines with medium body, bright red fruit flavors, and relatively low tannins
- **Growing Regions**: Extensively planted in Spain and France (particularly southern Rhône and Châteauneuf-du-Pape)
- **Planting Status**: One of the most widely planted red grape varieties globally, though Spanish plantings have declined from 420,000 to 203,000 acres since the 1980s
- **Versatility**: Used in red blends, rosés (especially Spanish rosado), and fortified wines

These five varieties represent some of the world's most important and widely cultivated wine grapes, each with distinct characteristics that contribute to their popularity and adaptability across different winemaking regions and styles.

<title>International Organisation of Vine and Wine</title>
<fragment>

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]

The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]




## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]

The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]




## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]



## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).


</fragment>

A common factor affecting Bordeaux wines' flavours is Cabernet Sauvignon's harvest yields. Throughout Bordeaux, there is a legal maximum permitted yield of 50 hectoliters (hl) per hectare (ha). With the aid of global warming and vigorous rootstocks, many Bordeaux vineyards can easily surpass 60 hl/ha, with some estates taking advantage of the legal loophole of *plafond limite de classement* ("ceiling limit classification") that permits higher yields during "exceptional" years. This has had an adverse effect on the quality of production from some producers who regularly use grapes harvested at excessive yields. In recent years there has been more of an emphasis on keeping yields low, particularly for an estate's *Grand vin*.[3]

Along with Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petit Verdot, Merlot is one of the primary grapes used in Bordeaux wine, and it is the most widely planted grape in the Bordeaux wine regions. Merlot is also one of the most popular red wine varietals in many markets.[2] This flexibility has helped to make it one of the world's most planted grape varieties. As of 2004, Merlot was estimated to be the third most grown variety at 260,000 hectares (640,000 acres) globally.[3]
The area planted to Merlot has continued to increase, with 266,000 hectares (660,000 acres) in 2015.[4]

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]

The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]

<fragment>
The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).


</fragment>

A common factor affecting Bordeaux wines' flavours is Cabernet Sauvignon's harvest yields. Throughout Bordeaux, there is a legal maximum permitted yield of 50 hectoliters (hl) per hectare (ha). With the aid of global warming and vigorous rootstocks, many Bordeaux vineyards can easily surpass 60 hl/ha, with some estates taking advantage of the legal loophole of *plafond limite de classement* ("ceiling limit classification") that permits higher yields during "exceptional" years. This has had an adverse effect on the quality of production from some producers who regularly use grapes harvested at excessive yields. In recent years there has been more of an emphasis on keeping yields low, particularly for an estate's *Grand vin*.[3]

Merlot is also one of the most popular red wine varietals in many markets.[2] This flexibility has helped to make it one of the world's most planted grape varieties. As of 2004, Merlot was estimated to be the third most grown variety at 260,000 hectares (640,000 acres) globally.[3]
The area planted to Merlot has continued to increase, with 266,000 hectares (660,000 acres) in 2015.[4]

![](image) A 50-yr old Airén vine, from a vineyard near Carabaña (Madrid, Spain)
**Airén** is a variety of *Vitis vinifera*, a white grape commonly used in winemaking. This grape is native to Spain where it represents almost a quarter of all grapes grown. As of 2010, Airén was estimated to be the world's 3rd most grown grape variety in terms of planted surface, at 252,000 hectares (620,000 acres), down from 306,000 hectares (760,000 acres) in 2004, where it held 1st place, although it is almost exclusively found in Spain.[1] Since Airén tends to be planted at a low density, several other varieties (including Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot) are more planted in terms of number of vines.

A common factor affecting Bordeaux wines' flavours is Cabernet Sauvignon's harvest yields. Throughout Bordeaux, there is a legal maximum permitted yield of 50 hectoliters (hl) per hectare (ha). With the aid of global warming and vigorous rootstocks, many Bordeaux vineyards can easily surpass 60 hl/ha, with some estates taking advantage of the legal loophole of *plafond limite de classement* ("ceiling limit classification") that permits higher yields during "exceptional" years. This has had an adverse effect on the quality of production from some producers who regularly use grapes harvested at excessive yields. In recent years there has been more of an emphasis on keeping yields low, particularly for an estate's *Grand vin*.[3]

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]

The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]

<fragment>
The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).

- **International Spread**: These grapes have expanded globally, with Merlot notably increasing its planted area from 260,000 to 266,000 hectares in just over a decade
- **Regional Specialization**: Different varieties thrive in different terroirs, which has shaped their historical significance

<document>
<title>Muscadelle</title>
<content>
White wine grape variety

For the white French wine grape that is also known under the similar synonym of Muscadet, see Melon de Bourgogne.



| Muscadelle |
| --- |
| Grape (*Vitis*) |
| ![](image) |
| Color of berry skin | Blanc |
| Species | *Vitis vinifera* |
| Also called | see list of synonyms |
| Origin | France |
| VIVC number | 8182 |


**Muscadelle** is a white wine grape variety. It has a simple aroma of grape juice and raisins like grapes of the Muscat family of grapes, but it is unrelated. 


DNA analysis has indicated that Muscadelle is a cross between Gouais blanc and an unidentified grape variety.[1]



## Wine regions

[edit]

In France, it is a minor constituent in the dry and sweet wines of Bordeaux, such as Sauternes. It rarely makes up more than 10% of the blend, which is dominated by Sémillon and Sauvignon blanc. Throughout the 1990s and the beginning of the 21st century, plantings of the grape were falling. Some sweet wines from Monbazillac, on the other hand, can have a higher proportion of Muscadelle.


In Australia, the grape is used to make a fortified wine, now known as Topaque (formerly Tokay). Those made in the Rutherglen region generally receive considerable aging in hot cellars, leading to a maderised and oxidative character. A few other Australian wine regions, including the Barossa Valley, make similar wines. A few other Australian wineries use Muscadelle to make table wines in a similar way to French wineries. In accordance with an agreement reached with the EU, Australian producers phased out their use of the term Tokay by 2020, most choosing instead the name *Topaque* to represent this style.[2]


The name, Tokay, convinced some Australian producers that the grape was Pinot gris (which used to be called Tokay by producers in Alsace). Others thought the grape might have been Hárslevelű, one of the components of the famous Hungarian sweet wine Tokaji. However, it has been proven that Australian Tokay is Muscadelle.[*by whom?*]



## Synonyms

[edit]

Muscadelle is also known under the synonyms Angelicaut, Angelico, Blanc Cadillac, Blanche Douce, Bouillenc Muscat, Buillenc, Cadillac, Catape, Colle, Colle Musquette, Doucanelle, Douzanelle, Enfin, Guepie, Guilan Doux, Guilan Muscat, Guilan Musque, Guillan, Guillan Musque, Guinlhan Musque, Marmesie, Marseillais, Muscade, Muscadela, Muscadelle de Bordelais, Muscadet, Muscadet Doux, Muscalea, Muscat Fou, Musquette, Pedro Ximenes Krimsky, Raisimotte, Raisin de Musco, Raisinote, Raisinotte, Rousselou, Sauvignon à Gros Grains, Sauvignon Muscadelle, Sauvignon vert, Tokay, Vesparo, and White Angelica.[1]



## References

[edit]

1. ^ ***a*** ***b*** Muscadelle Archived 2012-05-13 at the Wayback Machine, Vitis International Variety Catalogue, accessed 2010-12-03
2. **^** "Homepage".

</content>

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]




## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]

The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).

msg.content:
<document>
<title>International Organisation of Vine and Wine</title>
<fragment>

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]




## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]



## References

[edit]

The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).


</fragment>
<fragment>

The current International Organisation of Vine and Wine was established following a 35-nation agreement on 3 April 2001, and replaced the International Vine and Wine Office. This agreement went into effect on 1 January 2004.[3]

The term *grape variety* refers to cultivars rather than actual botanical varieties according to the International Code of Nomenclature for Cultivated Plants, because they are propagated by cuttings and may have unstable reproductive properties. ![](image)Top 20 grape producing countries in 2012.[17]
According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), 75,866 square kilometers of the world are dedicated to grapes. Approximately 71% of world grape production is used for wine, 27% as fresh fruit, and 2% as dried fruit. A portion of grape production goes to producing grape juice to be reconstituted for fruits canned "with no added sugar" and "100% natural". The area dedicated to vineyards is increasing by about 2% per year.


There are no reliable statistics that break down grape production by variety. It is believed that the most widely planted variety is Sultana, also known as Thompson Seedless, with at least 3,600 km2 (880,000 acres) dedicated to it. The second most common variety is Airén. Other popular varieties include Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon blanc, Cabernet Franc, Merlot, Grenache, Tempranillo, Riesling, and Chardonnay.[18]

msg.content:
<document>
<title>International Organisation of Vine and Wine</title>
<fragment>

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]




## History

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]



## References

[edit]

The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).

"Wine grapes" redirects here. For the book, see Wine Grapes.

This **list of grape varieties** includes cultivated grapes, whether used for wine, or eating as a table grape, fresh or dried (raisin, currant, sultana). For a complete list of all grape species including those unimportant to agriculture, see Vitis.


The term *grape variety* refers to cultivars rather than actual botanical varieties according to the International Code of Nomenclature for Cultivated Plants, because they are propagated by cuttings and may have unstable reproductive properties. However, the term *variety* has become so entrenched in viticulture that any change to using the term *cultivar* instead is unlikely.




## Single species grapes

[edit]

While some of the grapes in this list[1][2][3][4][5] are hybrids, they are hybridized within a single species. For those grapes hybridized across species, known as interspecific hybrids, see the section on multispecies hybrid grapes below.

As the laws on provincial viticulture were relaxed, vast vineyards began to flourish in the rest of Europe, especially Gaul (present-day France) and Hispania. Depending on the vintage, modern Italy is the world's largest or second-largest wine producer. In 2005, production was about 20% of the global total, second only to France, which produced 26%. Based on my research from Wikipedia articles on major wine-producing countries, here's a comprehensive overview of **what grape varieties are most commonly grown across different countries**:

## **🍇 France**
France has strict regional rules, with specific grapes tied to particular appellations:

**Top varieties by area (2007):**
1. **Merlot** - 13.6% (116,715 ha) - Bordeaux
2. **Grenache** - 11.3% (97,171 ha) - Rhône Valley
3. **Ugni blanc** - 9.7% (83,173 ha) - Cognac region
4. **Syrah** - 8.1% (69,891 ha) - Rhône Valley
5. **Carignan** - 6.9% (59,210 ha) - Southern France
6. **Cabernet Sauvignon** - 6.7% (57,913 ha) - Bordeaux
7. **Chardonnay** - 5.1% (43,887 ha) - Burgundy, Champagne
8. **Cabernet Franc** - 4.4% (37,508 ha) - Loire Valley, Bordeaux

*Note: France has strict rules - e.g., no Cabernet Sauvignon in Rhône, no Riesling in Loire.*

## **🍷 Italy**
Italy is the world's largest or second-largest wine producer:

**Most significant varieties:**
- **Sangiovese** - Primary grape of Tuscany (Chianti, Brunello)
- **Montepulciano** - Central and southern Italy
- **Barbera** - Piedmont region
- **Primitivo** - Southern Italy
- **Nebbiolo** - Piedmont (Barolo, Barbaresco)
- **Trebbiano** - Widely planted white variety
- **Catarratto** - Sicily

## **🍷 Germany**
Germany specializes in white wines, particularly Riesling:

**Top varieties (2015):**
1. **Riesling** - 23.0% (23,596 ha) - Mosel, Rheingau, Palatinate
2. **Müller-Thurgau** - 12.4% (12,736 ha) - Rheinhessen, Baden
3. **Spätburgunder (Pinot Noir)** - 11.5% (11,784 ha) - Baden, Palatinate
4. **Dornfelder** - 7.7% (7,868 ha) - Rheinhessen, Palatinate
5. **Grauburgunder (Pinot Gris)** - 5.8% (5,947 ha) - Rheinhessen, Palatinate
6. **Silvaner** - 4.9% (4,977 ha) - Franconia, Rheinhessen

*White grapes account for 66% of German plantings*

## **🇪🇸 Spain**
Spain focuses on indigenous varieties alongside international grapes:

**Key regional varieties:**
- **Tempranillo** - Rioja, Ribera del Duero (Spain's noble red)
- **Airén** - La Mancha (one of world's most planted whites)
- **Garnacha (Grenache)** - Northeastern Spain
- **Monastrell (Mourvèdre)** - Southeastern Spain
- **Albariño** - Rías Baixas (northwest)
- **Verdejo** - Rueda
- **Palomino** - Andalusia (Sherry production)
- **Macabeo, Parellada, Xarel·lo** - Cava production regions

## **🇺🇸 United States**
The U.S. produces diverse varieties, with California leading:

**Major varieties:**
- **Cabernet Sauvignon** - California, especially Napa Valley
- **Chardonnay** - Widespread, particularly California
- **Merlot** - California, Washington
- **Pinot Noir** - Oregon, California
- **Zinfandel** - California's signature variety
- **Sauvignon Blanc** - California, Washington
- **Riesling** - Washington, New York Finger Lakes
- **Concord** - Native American variety (not Vitis vinifera)

## **🌍 Key Regional Patterns:**

**France & Italy**: Blend-based wines with strict regional rules
**Germany**: White wine dominance (66% white, 34% red)
**Spain**: Indigenous varieties with growing international varieties
**USA**: Mix of international varieties and some native grapes

**International varieties** (grown in multiple countries):
- **Cabernet Sauvignon** - France, USA, Italy, Spain
- **Chardonnay** - France, USA, Germany, Italy, Spain  
- **Merlot** - France, USA, Italy, Spain
- **Syrah/Shiraz** - France, USA, Spain
- **Sauvignon Blanc** - France, USA, Germany, Spain

Each country shows distinct preferences shaped by climate, tradition, and market demands, with France maintaining the most strict regional grape regulations and Germany showing the strongest white wine specialization.

Based on my search results through Wikipedia, I can provide you with information about the key differences between the white wine grape varieties you mentioned. However, I should note that the search results returned mainly reference sections and bibliographic information rather than the full descriptive content about these varieties. Let me provide you with the key differences based on general wine knowledge:

## **Sauvignon Blanc vs. Sémillon**

**Sauvignon Blanc:**
- **Aroma Profile:** Known for distinctive aromas of gooseberry, passion fruit, grapefruit, and herbaceous notes (grass, cut grass)
- **Acidity:** High, crisp acidity
- **Body:** Light to medium-bodied
- **Regions:** Famous from Loire Valley (France), Marlborough (New Zealand), California
- **Style:** Typically unoaked, fresh, and aromatic
- **Winemaking:** Often made in stainless steel to preserve fresh fruit character

**Sémillon:**
- **Aroma Profile:** More subtle - honey, lanolin, beeswax, citrus (lemon, grapefruit)
- **Acidity:** Medium acidity when young
- **Body:** Medium to full-bodied
- **Regions:** Famous from Bordeaux (France), Hunter Valley (Australia)
- **Style:** Can be made dry or used in dessert wines (Sauternes)
- **Winemaking:** Benefits from oak aging, develops nutty, honeyed character with age

## **Chardonnay**

**Chardonnay:**
- **Aroma Profile:** Versatile - ranges from green apple, citrus (unoaked) to butter, vanilla, toast (oaked)
- **Acidity:** Medium to high acidity
- **Body:** Medium to full-bodied
- **Regions:** Burgundy (France), California, Australia, Champagne
- **Style:** Can be unoaked (Chablis-style) or heavily oaked (California style)
- **Winemaking:** Very versatile - responds well to oak, malolactic fermentation, various aging techniques

## **Red Wine Comparison: Merlot vs. Malbec**

**Merlot:**
- **Aroma Profile:** Plum, black cherry, blackberry, chocolate, earthy notes
- **Tannins:** Softer, rounder tannins compared to Cabernet Sauvignon
- **Body:** Medium to full-bodied
- **Regions:** Bordeaux (France), California, Washington State, Chile
- **Style:** Approachable, smooth, often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon
- **Winemaking:** Can be aged in oak, develops complexity with age

**Malbec:**
- **Aroma Profile:** Dark fruit (plum, blackberry), cocoa, tobacco, leather
- **Tannins:** Moderate to high tannins, typically softer than Cabernet
- **Body:** Full-bodied
- **Regions:** Argentina (Mendoza), Cahors (France), Chile, California
- **Style:** Rich, inky dark color, lush fruit character
- **Winemaking:** Often aged in oak, benefits from warm climate conditions

## **Key Takeaways:**

1. **Sauvignon Blanc** is the most aromatic and acidic of the white varieties
2. **Sémillon** is the most subtle and age-worthy, especially in Bordeaux blends
3. **Chardonnay** is the most versatile in terms of winemaking styles
4. **Merlot** produces smoother, more approachable red wines
5. **Malbec** offers rich, dark fruit character with good structure

White wines are generally better served chilled, while red wines are typically served at room temperature, though the specific serving temperature can vary based on the wine's body and style.

1. **Ugni blanc** - 83,173 hectares (9.7% of total French plantings)

- **Sémillon ranks 5th** among white varieties with 11,864 hectares

<document>
<title>Muscadelle</title>
<content>
White wine grape variety

For the white French wine grape that is also known under the similar synonym of Muscadet, see Melon de Bourgogne.



| Muscadelle |
| --- |
| Grape (*Vitis*) |
| ![](image) |
| Color of berry skin | Blanc |
| Species | *Vitis vinifera* |
| Also called | see list of synonyms |
| Origin | France |
| VIVC number | 8182 |


**Muscadelle** is a white wine grape variety. It has a simple aroma of grape juice and raisins like grapes of the Muscat family of grapes, but it is unrelated. 


DNA analysis has indicated that Muscadelle is a cross between Gouais blanc and an unidentified grape variety.[1]



## Wine regions

[edit]

In France, it is a minor constituent in the dry and sweet wines of Bordeaux, such as Sauternes. It rarely makes up more than 10% of the blend, which is dominated by Sémillon and Sauvignon blanc. Throughout the 1990s and the beginning of the 21st century, plantings of the grape were falling. Some sweet wines from Monbazillac, on the other hand, can have a higher proportion of Muscadelle.


In Australia, the grape is used to make a fortified wine, now known as Topaque (formerly Tokay). Those made in the Rutherglen region generally receive considerable aging in hot cellars, leading to a maderised and oxidative character. A few other Australian wine regions, including the Barossa Valley, make similar wines. A few other Australian wineries use Muscadelle to make table wines in a similar way to French wineries. In accordance with an agreement reached with the EU, Australian producers phased out their use of the term Tokay by 2020, most choosing instead the name *Topaque* to represent this style.[2]


The name, Tokay, convinced some Australian producers that the grape was Pinot gris (which used to be called Tokay by producers in Alsace). Others thought the grape might have been Hárslevelű, one of the components of the famous Hungarian sweet wine Tokaji. However, it has been proven that Australian Tokay is Muscadelle.[*by whom?*]



## Synonyms

[edit]

Muscadelle is also known under the synonyms Angelicaut, Angelico, Blanc Cadillac, Blanche Douce, Bouillenc Muscat, Buillenc, Cadillac, Catape, Colle, Colle Musquette, Doucanelle, Douzanelle, Enfin, Guepie, Guilan Doux, Guilan Muscat, Guilan Musque, Guillan, Guillan Musque, Guinlhan Musque, Marmesie, Marseillais, Muscade, Muscadela, Muscadelle de Bordelais, Muscadet, Muscadet Doux, Muscalea, Muscat Fou, Musquette, Pedro Ximenes Krimsky, Raisimotte, Raisin de Musco, Raisinote, Raisinotte, Rousselou, Sauvignon à Gros Grains, Sauvignon Muscadelle, Sauvignon vert, Tokay, Vesparo, and White Angelica.[1]

![](image) A 50-yr old Airén vine, from a vineyard near Carabaña (Madrid, Spain)
**Airén** is a variety of *Vitis vinifera*, a white grape commonly used in winemaking. This grape is native to Spain where it represents almost a quarter of all grapes grown. As of 2010, Airén was estimated to be the world's 3rd most grown grape variety in terms of planted surface, at 252,000 hectares (620,000 acres), down from 306,000 hectares (760,000 acres) in 2004, where it held 1st place, although it is almost exclusively found in Spain.[1] Since Airén tends to be planted at a low density, several other varieties (including Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot) are more planted in terms of number of vines.

<title>International Organisation of Vine and Wine</title>
<fragment>

The **International Organisation of Vine and Wine** ([undefined] Error: {{Langx}}: no text (help); **OIV**) is an intergovernmental organization which deals with technical and scientific aspects of viticulture and winemaking.[1] The field of OIV includes grape production for all purposes, i.e. not just wine, but also table grapes and raisin production.


One of the activities of OIV is the compilation of global statistics within its field.


OIV is based in Dijon, and had 49 member states as of 2022.[2][3]

The International Organisation of Vine and Wine provides methods to assess the color of a wine using a spectrophotometer and the calculation of indices in the Lab color space.[6]



## Resolutions

[edit]

In 2013, the OIV took a resolution which "recommends obtaining and developing new cultivars which carry multiple resistance loci [...] to lower the risk of selection and of development of more aggressive pathogen strains", especially for downy and powdery mildew.[7]



## References

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The current International Organisation of Vine and Wine was established following a 35-nation agreement on 3 April 2001, and replaced the International Vine and Wine Office. This agreement went into effect on 1 January 2004.[3]

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
The earliest forerunners of the OIV are the international conferences held as a reaction to the 19th century phylloxera epidemic, with the five-nation Montpellier Congress held between 26 and 30 October 1874 being the foremost among these.[4] The idea of an international organization came up several times during the coming decades, and finally, on 29 November 1924, eight nations signed an agreement concerned with the creation of an International Wine Office (*Office international du vin*, OIV) in Paris. After that the agreement went back to nations for ratification. The first working session was held at Salon de l’Horloge on 3 December 1927. On 4 September 1958, the organization's name was changed to the International Vine and Wine Office (*Office International de la Vigne et du Vin*).

Along with Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, Malbec and Petit Verdot, Merlot is one of the primary grapes used in Bordeaux wine, and it is the most widely planted grape in the Bordeaux wine regions. Merlot is also one of the most popular red wine varietals in many markets.[2] This flexibility has helped to make it one of the world's most planted grape varieties. As of 2004, Merlot was estimated to be the third most grown variety at 260,000 hectares (640,000 acres) globally.[3]
The area planted to Merlot has continued to increase, with 266,000 hectares (660,000 acres) in 2015.[4]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In places like Israel, Merlot is the second most widely planted grape variety after Cabernet Sauvignon with 1,000 hectares (2,500 acres) in cultivation, making very "New World-style" wines. The grape can also be found in Turkey with 429 hectares (1,060 acres) in 2010 as well as Malta and Cyprus.[1]



### France

[edit]


</fragment>
<fragment>
Merlot is one of the world's most widely planted grape variety with plantings of the vine outpacing even the more well-known Cabernet Sauvignon in many regions, including the grape's homeland of France.[1] Here, France is home to nearly two thirds of the world's total plantings of Merlot.[10] Beyond France it is also grown in Italy (where it is the country's 5th most planted grape), Algeria,[11] California, Romania, Australia, Argentina, Bulgaria, Canada, Chile, Greece, New Zealand, South Africa, Switzerland, Croatia, Hungary, Montenegro, Slovenia, Mexico and other parts of the United States such as Washington, Virginia and Long Island. It grows in many regions that also grow Cabernet Sauvignon but tends to be cultivated in the cooler portions of those areas. In areas that are too warm, Merlot will ripen too early.[6]


</fragment>
